title: Conjunctive queries: syntax and semantics
lead: Relational calculus, CQ rules, substitutions, homomorphisms and query answers.

sections.title: Algebra and declarative query languages
sections.html:
Source database and the first two algebra queries

The theory lectures reuse a small database so each answer can be verified directly. Flight contains four tuples and Airport six:

origindestinationairline
VIELHRBA
LHREDIBA
LGWGLAU2
LCAVIEOS
codecity
VIEVienna
LHRLondon
LGWLondon
LCALarnaca
GLAGlasgow
EDIEdinburgh

Projecting Flight.airline yields the set {BA,U2,OS}; BA occurs in two flights but set projection removes repetition. Selecting Airport.city='London' and projecting code yields {LHR,LGW}. Do the selection before discarding city, because a projection that removes it would make that predicate unavailable.

PDF pp. 1–6

London to Glasgow: every intermediate result

Select the London airports LHR,LGW and the Glasgow airport GLA as two separately renamed Airport instances. Join Flight.origin to the London code: retain (LHR,EDI,BA) and (LGW,GLA,U2). Join their destination to Glasgow’s code: only (LGW,GLA,U2) remains. Project airline: {U2}.

Both airport instances are necessary: a single row cannot simultaneously have city London and Glasgow. The repeated pages progressively reveal the selected tables, first join, second join and final projection. The query asks direct flights, so a path such as London→Vienna→Glasgow would not qualify.

PDF pp. 7–11

From execution to mathematical foundations

The focus now shifts from physical evaluation to query meaning and complexity. Codd’s theorem connects relational algebra with the appropriate domain-independent relational calculus; unrestricted unsafe calculus is not an equivalent finite-query language. A declarative formulation states what must hold; the DBMS derives an executable plan.

PDF pp. 12–14

sections.title: CQ syntax: head and body
sections.html:
The same three queries in calculus

Airlines: {z | ∃x∃y Flight(x,y,z)}. Existential x,y hide endpoints while z remains output. London codes: {x | Airport(x,London)}. Direct airlines: {z | ∃x∃y (Airport(x,London) ∧ Airport(y,Glasgow) ∧ Flight(x,y,z))}. Reusing x,y enforces matching endpoints across atoms; London and Glasgow are fixed constants, not variables to choose. The answers remain {BA,U2,OS}, {LHR,LGW}, {U2}.

PDF pp. 15–17

CQ syntax and the rule notation

A conjunctive query has the form Q(x̄):=∃ȳ(R1(v̄1) ∧ … ∧ Rm(v̄m)), or Q(x̄) :- R1(v̄1),…,Rm(v̄m). The head contains distinguished/output variables; body-only variables are existential. Safe outputs occur in body atoms. Relation names and arities must agree with the schema; constants retain their identity.

This is the select–project–join fragment under set semantics, expressed with existential quantification and conjunction. Joins/equality can be represented by shared variables; constant selections by constants in atoms. It excludes negation, disjunction, universal quantification and arbitrary aggregates. SQL bag multiplicities and NULL semantics are not automatically this mathematical model.

PDF pp. 18–19

sections.title: The Flight/Airport source query
sections.html:
Writing the three source CQs

The first rule is Q(z) :- Flight(x,y,z); x,y are hidden. The second is Q(x) :- Airport(x,London). The third is:

Q(z) :- Airport(x,London), Airport(y,Glasgow), Flight(x,y,z)

Read the body as simultaneous requirements on one assignment, not as three unrelated lookups. For the third query, choosing an origin in London and a destination in Glasgow is insufficient unless the same x,y,z also satisfy Flight. The algebra, calculus and rule forms describe the same three set answers.

PDF pp. 20–23

Database facts as a pattern-matching target

Represent each stored tuple as a ground atom such as Airport(LGW,London) or Flight(LGW,GLA,U2). The query body is a pattern of atoms with variables; evaluation searches for one consistent substitution sending all its atoms into the database. A candidate x=LHR,y=GLA fails because no Flight(LHR,GLA,z) exists in this instance, even though both selected airport facts exist.

PDF pp. 24–25

sections.title: Substitutions and homomorphisms
sections.html:
Homomorphism: two conditions

A substitution h maps terms in A to terms in B. It is a homomorphism if (1) every constant c is fixed, h(c)=c, and (2) every atom R(t1,…,tk) in A maps to an atom R(h(t1),…,h(tk)) present in B. It preserves relation names, arities and repeated-variable equality.

It need not be injective or surjective: distinct variables can collapse to one target term, and B can contain unused atoms. Renaming a constant or mapping only some atoms fails the definition.

PDF pp. 26–27

Checking both source homomorphisms atom by atom

Let A={R(x,a,y),R(a,x,b),S(x,c,y),T(x,x,d)}. The target B contains R(b,a,c),R(a,a,b),R(a,b,b),S(a,c,b),S(b,c,c),T(a,a,d),T(b,b,d), where a,b,c,d are constants.

For h1:x→a,y→b, the image atoms are R(a,a,b),R(a,a,b),S(a,c,b),T(a,a,d), all in B; two different source atoms collapse. For h2:x→b,y→c, they are R(b,a,c),R(a,b,b),S(b,c,c),T(b,b,d), again all present. The atom R(a,b,b) is needed for h2’s second R, not R(b,a,c). Both mappings fix every constant.

PDF pp. 28–30

sections.title: Semantics of a CQ answer
sections.html:
From matches to answer tuples

A match is a homomorphism from the body to the database. Evaluate Q(x1,…,xk) by collecting (h(x1),…,h(xk)) for every match h; existential witnesses themselves are not output. Different matches yielding the same tuple contribute one tuple under set semantics.

For the flight rule, h(x) = LGW, h(y)=GLA, h(z)=U2, with London and Glasgow fixed. The three images Airport(LGW,London),Airport(GLA,Glasgow),Flight(LGW,GLA,U2) are stored facts. The distinguished variable is z, so output U2, not the whole assignment or the airport codes. This completes the source’s pattern-matching animation.

PDF pp. 31–33

quiz.question: In Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(y), what is y?
options: An existentially quantified variable shared by the two atoms
quiz.explanation: The variable y does not appear in the head, but every occurrence of y must receive the same value within an assignment.

source.summary: Lecture 23 connects relational algebra and calculus with conjunctive queries. It defines head and body syntax, homomorphisms, and result semantics in terms of matches.
